sweep_summary: Mohawk (moha1258) is in the catalog as fixed-strict (penult; deciding quote is the StressTyp2-style Bonvillain-based text, cite empty; our check store names Hagstrom 1997 as the deciding file we hold). All five title-keyword items are about Mohawk word stress; none has an open full text. Michelson 1981 (HSP 2) is print-only with no online record. Michelson 1983 (two duplicate Glottolog records for one Harvard dissertation) and Michelson 1988 (its published revision, Kluwer, DOI 10.1007/978-94-009-2709-4; paywalled, archive.org borrow-only, HathiTrust search-only) were reached only as Google Books snippets: 1983 §2.4 'Mohawk has preserved the PNI rule of penultimate stress.. made opaque in Mohawk by the operation of epenthesis rules'; 1988 ch.3 'The PLI pattern of penultimate accent and vowel lengthening in accented open penults has been preserved in Mohawk'. Potter 1994 (CLS 30:347-361, print only, not on ROA) snippet: 'stress is penultimate regardless of whether the penult and ultima syllables are open or closed.. Excrescent vowels in penultimate position are not stressed'. Every item confirms the fixed-strict penult coding with epenthetic-vowel invisibility. Best new first-hand statement: Michelson 1988 ch.3 snippet (does not supersede the current source because only a snippet without page was obtained); Michelson 1988 remains the high-priority acquisition. Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, archive.org, HathiTrust, Google Books, ROA and Springer were queried directly. Saved.

new_statements.quote: [sec. 2.4.11] ... stress is obligatory, however. All Mohawk words must contain one and only one stressed vowel. The determination of the placement of stress within the word is complex and will be discussed in detail in 3.7.1. below. Generally, though, stress is placed on the penultimate vowel. Most exceptions to this general rule can be accounted for by subsidiary rules which shift stress from the penultimate to a preceding vowel (see 3.7.2. for the conditions of this adjustment.). [sec. 3.7.21 'Stress'] The problem of the placement of stress within the word is very complex. However, a few patterns can be pointed out here ... To begin with, the preferred syllable to receive stress is the penultimate. A word of more than one syllable spoken in isolation is very rarely stressed on the final syllable. Monosyllabic words are extremely rare. 3.7.22. The rule placing stress on the penultimate syllable must apply before the application of two additional morphophonemic rules. The first such rule supplies epenthetic vowels.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every Mohawk word has exactly one stressed vowel; stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel; surface exceptions (stress on an earlier vowel, e.g. the antepenult) arise because penultimate stress placement is ordered before two morphophonemic insertion rules (e-epenthesis and the joiner/filler vowel -a-), so inserted vowels can follow the stressed vowel; final stress in polysyllables spoken in isolation is very rare; monosyllables are extremely rare (a prothetic vowel is added to potential monosyllables).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'All Mohawk words must contain one and only one stressed vowel' (sec. 2.4.11); no secondary stress is described in the snippets seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifted from the penult to a preceding vowel by subsidiary rules (sec. 3.7.2: epenthetic e and the morpheme joiner -a- inserted after stress placement); rare words with final stress (one loan-like word 'unusual in that the final vowel is stressed', sec. 3.7.x); monosyllables extremely rare.
new_statements.identity_note: Bonvillain describes the Akwesasne (St. Regis) dialect of Mohawk; Potter's data are Mohawk without a dialect visible in the snippets (he cites G. Michelson 1973 A Thousand Words of Mohawk).

new_statements.quote: II. An Analysis of the Basic Prosodic Phenomena. Stress in Mohawk regularly surfaces on the penultimate syllable. Examples (1a)-(1d) illustrate that stress is penultimate regardless of whether the penult and ultima syllables are open or closed. Stressed open syllables include a long vowel. [...] With NonFinality ranked above Edgemost and violations of Edgemost calculated cumulatively in terms of distance of the stressed syllable from the right edge of the word, the optimal location of stress in Mohawk words is on the penultimate syllable. [p.352:] Excrescent vowels in penultimate position are not stressed (21), unlike epenthetic vowels which do surface with stress in penultimate position (22). [p.353:] Unlike other underlying vowels, the joiner vowel is not stressed in open syllables in penultimate position.

new_statements.relation_note: Same penultimate placement as the catalog's fixed-strict coding and its StressTyp2/Bonvillain quote (one stress, penult, inserted vowels can displace surface stress to the antepenult); consistent with Michelson 1988 and the Potter snippet statement already held by the project, now verified against the full text with page numbers; adds the excrescent-vs-epenthetic e and joiner-vowel conditions and open-penult lengthening (refining detail, no conflict).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable (NonFinality: the head foot may not include the word-final syllable, outranking Edgemost-Right), whether penult/ultima are open or closed; a stressed open-syllable vowel is lengthened. Prothetic i- and true epenthetic e are visible to stress; excrescent e (C[-glottal]_[+son], C_ʔ) is invisible: unstressable in the penult, no lengthening trigger, does not count for the disyllabic minimum; the stem-joiner -a- is unstressed in an open penult (stress then antepenultimate, with lengthening) but stressed in a closed penult or after an excrescent e. Stress correlates with phonetic high tone (p.359).
new_statements.secondary_stress: not discussed; constraints refer only to the primary stressed syllable / main foot
new_statements.exceptions: excrescent e in the penult is skipped (tékeriks 'I put side by side' vs epenthetic wakényaks 'I get married'); open-penult joiner vowel unstressed -> antepenultimate stress (tehsa?á:rarik 'Close the curtains!'), but stressed when the penult is closed (kyʌtákwas 'I collect wood') or preceded by excrescent e (teka?nukserá:ke 'two onions', after Michelson 1988); word-level stress position preserved across derivational levels
new_statements.identity_note: Bonvillain describes the Akwesasne (St. Regis) dialect of Mohawk; Potter's data are Mohawk without a dialect visible in the snippets (he cites G. Michelson 1973 A Thousand Words of Mohawk).

sources.note: Second-hand theoretical (OT) analysis of Mohawk stress and epenthesis, data from Michelson: stress is regularly penultimate, quantity-insensitive (penult and ultima open or closed), stressed open syllables lengthen, and excrescent (epenthetic) e in penult position is skipped. Hagstrom 1997 (held) quotes Potter 1994:354 for the hypothesis that the epenthetic vowel's mora is not dominated by a syllable node and only syllables are footed. Confirms the fixed-strict penult coding with the epenthesis caveat.
